question: 1313. Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the funding measures available for community groups to apply for funding for CCTV facilities in community facilities/amenities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [41816/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Community safety is a top priority for my Department and everyone has the right to be safe and to feel safe in their communities. CCTV in public places has a role in giving people a greater sense of security. It can also be effective in deterring criminal activity and antisocial behaviour and assists with the investigation of crime. Since 2017 my Department has administered a grant-aid scheme supporting groups wishing to establish a community-based CCTV system in their area, which provides grants of up to €40,000 for capital expenditure and up to €5,000 for maintenance. This scheme was extended in 2019 to cover not only new CCTV systems, but to also provide funding for the extension or upgrade of existing CCTV systems which are incomplete or obsolete. Grants of over €968,000 have been approved to date for 36 Community CCTV schemes. The consideration and operation of community CCTV by local authorities is a matter for the local authority concerned. As Minister, I have no role in local authorities and updates on the rollout of individual community CCTV schemes should be sought from the relevant local authority. The Garda National Community Engagement Bureau offer support and assistance in relation to all applications and processes. Each application is evaluated on the principles of necessity, proportionality, legality and therefore receives the necessary and robust review to ensure the CCTV application will withstand a Human Rights and Privacy screening test. All applications must be presented to the CCTV Advisory Committee and the need for each camera justified. The Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023 provides for a new regime for the authorisation and operation of CCTV schemes. Part 5 of that Act, when commenced, will introduce these new arrangements. There is a requirement under that Act for the Garda Commissioner to develop a Code of Practice for CCTV which will set out the procedures to be followed. As part of developing this new Code of Practice, An Garda Síochána consulted with the bodies listed in Part 8 of the Act and conducted a public consultation to seek submissions for any views or observations on the draft Code of Practice for Part 5. This consultation period ended on 24 February 2026. Prior to commencement, an amendment is also required to the transitional arrangements in section 7 of the 2023 Act, for existing CCTV applications. That amendment has been included in the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) (Amendment) Bill and is currently before the Houses of the Oireachtas. I expect that the new CCTV provisions set out in Part 5 will be commenced this summer.

question: 1322. Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he intends to go through the planning process as outlined in the Planning and Development Act 2000 for the new Cork prison on the old Cork prison site; or if he intends to bring this forward as legislation as was done previously with the Cork prison that opened in 2016. [41986/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under Irish law, major state infrastructure for national security and penal administration is generally exempt from standard planning permissions managed by local authorities. This legislative approach allows the State to expedite critical national infrastructure. The new Cork Prison facility, which officially opened in 2016 adjacent to the old prison, was not brought forward through the local planning process. Instead, it was developed purely through the use of state legislation. The project was delivered by the Irish Prison Service under the specific provisions of the Prisons Acts (including the Prisons Act 2007) and in line with the then modernisation programme mainly due to the risks inherent in the old facility and to provide in cell sanitation to the Cork prison population. The proposed project for the extension to the existing Cork Prison is still at an early stage with the exact specifics and approach yet to be determined.

question: 1323. Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the transfer of River Lodge, Newtownmountkennedy from his Department to the HSE; the timeline for the site to be returned to the HSE; the costs associated with the site since 2025; the status of any existing contracts with providers at the site, including security; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [41999/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration River Lodge, Newtownmountkennedy was offered to IPAS by the HSE in February 2024 and used to provide tented emergency accommodation during a time of increased pressure on the international protection system. The cost of establishing the site as an accommodation centre was approximately €400,000. Accommodation was provided from early May to December 2024. The site provided tented accommodation with capacity for 96 residents. Due to severe weather conditions in December 2024, residents had to be moved from the site to alternative accommodation. A process to explore alternative development options to potentially repurpose River Lodge for other forms of accommodation was carried out. Following technical and financial assessments - particularly in relation to wastewater treatment infrastructure - it was deemed not possible to move forward with such proposals. It has been agreed with the HSE that the site will be returned to them, bringing the licensed use of this site for IPAS accommodation to a conclusion. question: 1324. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total number of knives seized by Gardaí in each county in the State over the past ten years; to provide a county-by-county breakdown on the figure; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42013/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1324, 1433 and 1434 together. The Government is committed to ensuring that communities are safe and tackling knife crime remains an important part of that work. Ireland has a comprehensive and robust legal framework in place to address knife crime, with penalties for knife-related offences strengthened in recent years. In 2024, legislation increased the maximum penalty for offences including possession of a knife with intent to cause injury, trespassing with a knife and producing a knife to unlawfully intimidate another person from five years to seven years imprisonment. In addition, the Government doubled the maximum penalty for assault causing harm to ten years imprisonment in 2023. While any incident involving a knife is deeply concerning, the available evidence does not support claims of a wider increase in knife-related offending. An Garda Síochána’s analysis of Knife Related Crime from 2015–2024 shows that assaults causing harm involving a knife accounted for, on average, less than 7% of all assault causing harm incidents over the past decade. The analysis also identified a 40% reduction in robberies involving a knife in retail spaces and a 35% reduction in robberies involving a knife in public spaces since 2020. An Garda Síochána continues to undertake a range of proactive measures to tackle assaults in public places, including those involving knives. This is informed by a pro-arrest, early-investigation and high-visibility policing approach. Tackling knife crime requires a sustained, evidence-based approach that addresses wider issues such as anti-social behaviour, street violence and youth offending. The Department is supporting this work through youth justice measures and through the establishment of Local Community Safety Partnerships, which bring together a broad range of stakeholders including local communities, youth, education, new and minority communities, the business community and public services and An Garda Síochána to address community safety issues at local level. An Garda Síochána's report on Knife Related Crime for 2015-2024 provides detailed analysis of incidents involving the use and/ or possession of a knife. The report is publicly available on the Garda website and I an informed by Garda authorities that it will be updated later in 2026. The report can be viewed at the below link: (www.garda.ie/en/about-us/publications/general-reports/knife-related-crime-2015-to-2024.pdf). Statistics on number of knives seized, by Garda Division, are available on page 14 of the report.

question: 1325. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of reported instances of intimidating drug debt collection reported in each county in the State last year. [42014/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government is fully committed to providing An Garda Síochána with the resources it needs to fight organised crime and the illegal drugs trade. This is reflected in the unprecedented allocation of over €2.74 billion in Budget 2026. Drug Related Intimidation is a high priority for An Garda Síochána. An Garda Síochána continues to maintain the Drugs Related Intimidation Reporting Programme - Garda (DRIRP) by assigning nominated Inspectors throughout the country to assist those who are victims of intimidation. An Garda Síochána is committed to continuing to build and maintain relationships with communities, agencies and groups in the fight against drug related intimidation and violence within all communities. An Garda Síochána recognises the important roles many different agencies and groups play in tackling the cause and symptoms of drug-related intimidation and violence. An Garda Síochána also continue to show this commitment by working with the Drug and Alcohol Task Forces nationwide who make up the DRIVE network. The anonymity afforded to victims through the service provided by An Garda Síochána by way of the Drug-Related Intimidation Reporting Programme is one of the key ways in which people are encouraged to report. As such, I am informed by the Garda authorities that data collected by An Garda Síochána, including relating to the number of reports for Drug Related Intimidation received, must be considered confidential.

question: 1328. Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of gardaí recruited to work in County Mayo in each of the past ten years; and the number of gardaí who have left the force in County Mayo in each of those years, in tabular form. [42018/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Gardaí nationally, including a breakdown of Garda divisions and stations nationwide. Historical data on the allocation of of Gardaí and probationer Gardaí from 2015 - 2025 can be found here: (www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html ). The Deputy should select December 2025 and then select the filed titled 'Allocation of Probationer Gardai" and "Garda Member by Division District Station" to access the relevant data. The allocation of each intake of newly attested probationer Gardaí is considered by the Commissioner in the context of the overall operational needs and policing priorities of the organisation, whilst also having regard to the resourcing requirements of each Garda Division. It is also important to note that the allocation of Probationer Gardaí is one part of the overall picture. Another part is the transfer of serving Gardaí to their preferred location which is facilitated by the attestation and allocation of a Probationer Gardaí. I am assured by the Garda Commissioner that, when allocating and transferring Gardaí to and from any Division, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. The requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide are also taken into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads • Policing arrangements and operational strategies • Local population and trends, geographical area and size • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. Newly attested Gardaí are allocated to specially designated training stations which have the required training and development structures and resources in place, including trained Garda tutors and access to a permanently appointed supervisory Sergeant who is thoroughly familiar with their responsibilities under the training programme. question: 1332. Deputy Claire Kerrane asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current estimated wait time for applicants for type D family reunification visas; the additional resourcing requirements that are being considered or have been implemented, to deal with the current visa backlog; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42084/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that my Department currently operates seven overseas Visa Offices in addition to the Visa Office in Dublin. These are located in Abuja, Beijing, London, Moscow, Ankara, Abu Dhabi and New Delhi. In addition, staff of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade process certain visa applications in Irish Embassies abroad under delegated authority from my Department. The current processing times of applications for join family visas varies depending on the circumstances when the application is made. If a non-EEA national is moving to Ireland because they have been granted a Critical Skills Employment Permit they can apply for join family visas at the same time as their own employment visa. When these visas are applied for together, they are processed in tandem and are typically completed in under eight weeks. My Department aims to process join family visa applications made in other circumstances within 12 months. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification. The majority of join family visas receive a first instance decision within this business target. In 2025 the average processing time for all types of Join Family visa applications was 113 days. Processing times and decisions at the Visa Offices in Dublin and overseas can be checked at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions. In December 2025, the Immigration Service of my Department introduced online payment functionality to my Department's online visa system. This allows applicants to pay visa fees as part of the online application process. The initiative is being rolled out on a phased basis and is currently live in 40 countries, with South Africa added in January 2026. This reduces the administrative burden on Irish Missions and visa teams, and allows visa officers to dedicate more time to core application processing and decision-making, contributing to improved processing efficiency over time. Furthermore, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated teams for Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing are intended to help streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving the service delivery for join family visa applications.

question: 1333. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration given the failure of Government to appointment a new Master of the High Court, the steps he has taken, or will take, to ensure the smooth administration of justice should the deputy master be unavailable; and if he will make a statement on the matter. answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1333 and 1334 together. question: 1335. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of prosecutions in total thus far initiated by Gardaí for breaches of regulations under the Health (Preservation and Protection and other Emergency Measures in the Public Interest) Act 2020; the number of such prosecutions currently pending or being pursued by the courts; and to provide a breakdown of the offences these prosecutions are for; the number of convictions secured to date; the total number of jail sentences imposed to date; the total number of court-imposed fines; and the total monetary value of those fines. [42105/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I have requested the information sought by the Deputy from the Garda authorities. Regrettably, this was not available in time and I will write to the Deputy once the information is to hand.

question: 1336. Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the process whereby a facility is scheduled to transition to a processing centre in the coming weeks; whether a curfew will be introduced given that none of the new residents will be expected to be working during this period; whether consideration can be given to indoor and outdoor socialising areas in their own right (details supplied); his plans for an on-site shop and post office; the consideration being given to short term educational needs for children of school going age on-site, given the short duration, or English language and cultural lessons for older temporary residents; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42114/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1336 and 1337 together. The Department’s International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) provides accommodation to people seeking international protection. People who are accommodated in IPAS accommodation centres are free to come and go from their accommodation. The purchase of the Citywest property is a key part of the Government’s strategy to develop a stable and sustainable accommodation system for people seeking international protection by moving away from commercial properties to State-owned centres. There is an ongoing community engagement programme in place in Citywest, where officials from my Department engage with representatives from the local community and local elected representatives to hear about and work to resolve local service matters that arise. A number of thematic issues and suggestions to strengthen public services and local infrastructure have been raised during these engagements, as have concerns about antisocial behaviour in the locality. Officials in my Department and centre management continue to work very closely with An Garda Síochána in the area to keep all issues raised under review. In relation to residents who have to move from one IPAS centre to another, this happens regularly for operational reasons, and if a family are moving with school-age children, supports are provided by the IPAS resident welfare team to ensure school places, if affected, can be established in the new area. The new International Protection Bill 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and was passed into law last month. The new rules will take effect on 12 June 2026. The Pact will provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for first-instance decisions: six months for the standard procedure, three months for the accelerated procedure and two months for the examination to determine whether an application is inadmissible. This gives status to those who are entitled to international protection to rebuild their lives here, while also ensuring faster decision making in respect of those who do not meet the criteria. Faster processing under the Pact will mean that applicants spend less time in IPAS accommodation, and this will significantly reduce the cost of the asylum system to the State. The Department is working, as part of the implementation plan for the Pact, to identify support services, existing and new, that applicants will require, under the new arrangements that will begin from later this week.

question: 1338. Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the future plans for the Ukrainian residents currently at a facility (details supplied) in terms of the length of time they are guaranteed accommodation; whether their employment and school needs will be facilitated in terms of future accommodation on a staggered basis while the occupation of Ukraine continues; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42116/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that, in line with recent Government decisions, a phased withdrawal of State-contracted accommodation for Ukrainians is underway. This includes the setting named by the Deputy. These changes to the accommodation model will be introduced on a phased basis, with information and support provided to residents. Vulnerable individuals who want to continue to avail of state-supported accommodation will be asked to self-declare their need for continued accommodation detailing their reasons with supporting evidence. An application process will open later in June. Details on the application process will be available in the coming weeks. While efforts will be made to keep people who fled the war in Ukraine as local as possible, this will not always be possible, particularly in light of the reduced accommodation portfolio. It is not possible to take issues such as employment or school places into account when allocating follow-on accommodation. People will be encouraged to make their own arrangements if they wish to stay in their current area, with some supports available to do so. Plans are advancing in respect of the accommodation named by the Deputy. Further details will be made available as plans are finalised. My Department will aim to ensure that residents are informed of impending changes in sufficient time for onward arrangements to be made.

question: 1339. Deputy Paul Nicholas Gogarty asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the communications he has received from the Garda Commissioner or local Superintendent of actions being taken to deal with antisocial behaviour in a location (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42117/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I engage regularly with the Garda Commissioner to ensure our Gardaí have the resources they need. The Garda Vote in Budget 2026 includes unprecedented funding of €2.74 billion which will support the continued recruitment of Garda personnel. This allocation demonstrates the Government’s commitment to ensuring An Garda Síochána has provision for the equipment, technology, facilities, fleet and personnel it needs to carry out vital policing work. I am advised that the Dublin Metropolitan Region (DMR) West Division, which includes Saggart and the wider Citywest area, has 728 Garda members assigned to it. The Division's resources are kept under ongoing review having regard to crime trends, population growth and operational demands. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, including the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel. Decisions regarding patrols, including the deployment of high-visibility or 24-hour patrols, are operational matters for the Commissioner and local Garda management. High-visibility patrols are a core element of community policing and form part of Garda operations, including targeted initiatives aimed at deterring crime and supporting community safety. Local Garda management engages with community stakeholders and public representatives in identifying policing priorities within the area. As part of those engagements and in other fora, community members and elected representatives have raised suggestions about local services. These suggestions include the potential development of a new Garda Station in Saggart as part of the Citywest campus that is now in State ownership. This and other suggestions will be considered in the context of the Government's commitment to listening to local people and leaders and helping to support the delivery of services in the area. An Garda Siochana introduced a High Visibility Policing (HPV) Plan in Dublin City Centre in March 2025. This initiative has since been rolled out to Cork and Limerick City Centres, as well as areas of South Dublin, including Tallaght and Dún Laoghaire. The Garda Commissioner is committed to continuing this rollout to other areas of the Dublin Metropolitan Region, and to other areas nationwide. Ongoing Garda recruitment is supporting this commitment. Feedback from business and the public on the High Visibility Policing approach in Dublin and the other cities where it has been introduced has been very positive, and I look forward to it being rolled out to other areas into the future. I will continue to engage with the Commissioner regarding the policing needs of communities.

question: 1340. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total amount spent by his Department on public procurement in 2025; to provide a breakdown, where available, by goods, services, works procurement expenditure, by expenditure procured directly by his Department and expenditure procured through central purchasing arrangements or frameworks; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42173/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1340 and 1341 together. I can inform the Deputy that expenditure on goods, professional services and other contracted services by my Department amounted to a total of €2,181,602,000 in 2025. In line with commitments made in the Programme for Government, responsibility for integration, International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS), and the Ukraine Division transferred to my Department from the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, and Equality on 1 May 2025. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) also transferred to my Department from the Department of the Environment, Communications and Climate on 1 June 2025. The above figure includes expenditure incurred for these functions from the point they became part of my Department. Public procurement is governed by EU and national rules and my Department ensures that appropriate procedures are followed for procurement activity. Departments are obliged to ensure that public procurement is discharged in line with the standard accounting and procurement rules and that contract prices represent best value for money. Public procurement practices are subject to audit and scrutiny under the Comptroller and Auditor General (Amendment) Act 1993. Procurement is also subject to internal audit within my Department. Department of Finance Circular 40/02 requires Government Departments and Offices to submit an annual report to the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General for contracts above €25,000 (exclusive of VAT), awarded without a competitive process, by 31 March of the following year and details of contracts awarded by my Department without the use of a competitive process are outlined in the Department’s Appropriation Accounts. I can assure the Deputy that my Department’s policy and practise is to use National Frameworks where they are available. The use of these frameworks helps to ensure that the aggregate purchasing power of the State is utilised to achieve value for money outcomes. Where suitable external frameworks are not available, the Department manages “in-house” procurement projects. My Department relies heavily on the use of Office of Government Procurement (OGP) Frameworks and the assistance of the OGP to drawdown from these Frameworks. The Deputy will be aware that under Circular 09/2024, Government Departments are required to report where they do not avail of central Frameworks. My Department is currently preparing its 2025 return for submission in advance of the deadline of 1 July next, and while only provisional at this time, I am pleased to inform the Deputy that my Department used OGP Frameworks, where available, for the majority of its requirements. I can also assure the Deputy that my Department is fully committed to the principles of openness, transparency and the accountability of public bodies. The Freedom of Information (FOI) Act (2014) establishes a structure to support the regular publication of details relating to the activities and spending of public bodies. Under section 8 of the Act, bodies are required to publish a scheme, having regard to the model scheme published by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. This model scheme includes the publication of purchase orders for both goods and services of €20,000 or over, or in the case of the HSE €100,000, on a quarterly basis. As the Deputy is aware the model is a guide and not a requirement and specifically provides for each public body to publish their own FOI scheme which may differ. My Department publishes all purchase orders of €20,000 or over on its website at the following link - www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/department-of-justice-purchase-orders-issued-over-20000-in-value/. As the Deputy may also be aware, my Department moved from annual to quarterly publication of purchase order data in 2025, with the most recently published data relating to – Q1 2026. While my Department publishes purchase order data, it does not currently compile/ publish the data referred to by the Deputy in the format sought, however, officials in my Department have begun a process to identify a suitable replacement solution for our current contract management information system used to record contract details. I understand that this includes consideration being given to aligning reporting from any new system with the requirements detailed in section E of the Model Publication Scheme Guidance.

question: 1342. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will review the case of a person (details supplied); if the certificate in question could be issued in the manner outlined; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42223/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that attendance at a Citizenship Ceremony is the final step in completing the naturalisation process. At a ceremony, applicants are required to sign the declaration of fidelity to the nation and loyalty to the state, and swear the oath of fidelity before a Presiding Officer appointed by me, as Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. Where a person is unable to attend a Ceremony, such as for medical reasons, they may seek to conclude their application via the affidavit declaration process. This process is only used in exceptional circumstances and applications are considered on a case by case basis. Applications to complete the naturalisation application via an affidavit can be made through the Department's Customer Service Portal and supporting evidence should be submitted with the request. The Customer Service Portal can be accessed at the following link: www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ . My Department strives to provide the best service possible to all applicants, including those with disabilities. At each Citizenship Ceremony, supports and assistance are provided to any person who may need it. Any supports and assistance can be requested when registering and responding to the invitation to attend the ceremony. Furthermore, an Access Officer is available and is responsible for providing, arranging and co-ordinating assistance to people with disabilities who wish to access the services provided by my Department. The Access Officer also acts as a point of contact for people with disabilities who wish to access such services. The Access Officer can be contacted by email at accessofficer@justice.ie or by phone 00 353 1 602 8202. When cases are identified that a person may have difficulties accessing a service or need reasonable accommodations due to their personal circumstances, officials will endeavour to assist them on a case-by-case basis as appropriate.

question: 1343. Deputy Shane Moynihan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which funds are allocated from seized funds by the Criminal Assets Bureau. [42233/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration CAB is a multi-agency statutory body established under the Criminal Assets Bureau Act, 1996. I am advised that all monies seized by CAB are remitted to the Central Fund of the Exchequer after the appropriate statutory time frame under the Proceeds of Crime Acts. Figures relating to asset recovery under the Proceeds of Crime Acts by CAB are available publicly in the annual reports published on the Bureau's website: www.cab.ie/annual-reports/ The disbursement of monies collected by the Criminal Assets Bureau is controlled by the Central Exchequer. However, the Deputy may be interested to note that the Community Safety Fund re-directs the proceeds of crime, seized by the Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB) and An Garda Síochána, back into communities in order to fund innovative local projects aimed at building stronger, safer communities. In 2025, €4.4 million was allocated through the Community Safety Fund to 42 community safety projects nationwide. This represented a 33% increase on the €3 million awarded in 2024. I secured a further increase in funding to €4.75 million for 2026, which is reflective of the continued success of An Garda Síochána and CAB. Putting this money back into the community is a tangible way of showing that there can be a direct link between the activities of law enforcement and building stronger, safer communities.

question: 1344. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of domestic violence refuge spaces currently available across the Midlands region, including Longford and Westmeath; whether additional refuge or family support accommodation is planned; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42244/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration This Government has taken unprecedented actions to confront the scourge of domestic, sexual, and gender-based violence (DSGBV). This includes increasing funding to almost €80 million under Budget 2026, to support Cuan and services working to tackle DSGBV and the implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. The increased funding for Cuan and community organisations that support victims and survivors will accelerate the delivery of safe accommodation, while also providing stronger supports for victims. Cuan is collaborating with various stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and Local Authorities to facilitate local action and support service development and delivery of safe accommodation and ancillary services. In the Midlands region, the following safe accommodation units are in place; in Longford there is one safe home unit, in Westmeath there are five domestic violence refuge units, in Roscommon there are two safe home units, and in Offaly there are three safe home units. These units of safe accommodation are available to anyone fleeing domestic violence, regardless of which county they are from. In Westmeath, progress has been made in the development of a domestic violence refuge, with a project manager in place and a design team selected. Once complete, this domestic violence refuge will have 12 units available. In Laois, the service provider leading the development of a domestic violence refuge is formalising partnership with an appointed Approved Housing Body (AHB). Once complete, this refuge will have 10 units available. Separately, Cuan is working closely with Roscommon Safe Link to increase the number of safe homes operating in County Roscommon and are actively pursuing potential properties. While almost three quarters of the population in the State is currently within 30 minutes of a refuge location, Cuan is acutely aware of the need to improve on this and to ensure that services are accessible to everyone living in rural and urban areas. Achieving this, including through the completion of a National Services Development Plan, is a core objective of Cuan’s Corporate Plan 2025-2027, which was published at the end of last year.

question: 1345. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of bicycle shelters installed across the State by his Department on behalf of Government Departments, local authorities, and State agencies in each of the past five years; the total expenditure incurred in each year; the average cost per unit; and if he will provide a breakdown by Department, local authority and agency. [42263/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department conducts its operations predominantly in buildings which are either owned or leased by the Office of Public Works (OPW) on behalf of my Department. I understand that details of all bicycle shelters installed across the State and procured by the OPW, have previously been provided to the Deputy in a response to Parliamentary Question 512 of 26 May 2026, answered by the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. In addition to the bicycle shelters procured by the OPW, I can confirm that my Department installed one bicycle shelter at a departmental office in Hanover Street, Dublin in 2022. The total cost for this shelter was €18,212.63 (ex. VAT). Further, I am informed by the Courts Service that, as part of works within the Dublin Estate, a bicycle shelter was installed at Chancery Street Courthouse in 2025, for a total cost of €7,882.40. Finally, I can confirm that the Irish Prison Service installed a designated bicycle shelter for staff in Castlerea Prison in 2022, for a total cost of €28,008.68 (ex. VAT).

question: 1346. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total amount spent on IT systems and related projects by his Department and agencies under its remit in each of the past five years; to provide a detailed breakdown of all such projects, including original budget, final cost, and delivery timelines; the number and value of projects that exceeded their original budget or timeline; the number and total cost of projects that were cancelled, abandoned, or failed to go live; the current status of all ongoing ICT projects with a value of €100,000 or greater, excluding routine operational spend (details supplied); and the governance, oversight, and risk management processes in place to prevent cost overruns and project failures. [42290/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It has not been possible to provide the information requested in the time provided. I will write to the Deputy directly once this information is available.

question: 1347. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to implement any of the recommendations of the report by the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Assisted Dying during the term of this Government; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42302/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The issue of assisted dying is very complex, requiring careful consideration of medical, ethical and cultural issues. It also gives rise to challenging issues in the areas of criminal justice and constitutional law. The Joint Committee on Assisted Dying was established in January 2023 to consider and make recommendations for legislative and policy change in relation to assisted dying. The Committee published its Final Report on 20 March 2024. The Committee’s report recommends that the Government introduce legislation to allow for assisted dying in certain restricted circumstances. On 23 October 2024, the Dáil voted by 76 to 53 to note the Committee’s Report. It is a matter for Government, on foot of the Dáil vote, to determine how to progress this issue, including with regard to which Department will take a lead role in relation to it. No decision has been taken, as of yet, as regards any proposed legislative, or other actions, to be taken.

question: 1348. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of humanitarian visa or family reunification cases involving residents of Longford and Westmeath currently being processed by his Department. [42311/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the deputy that my Department does not collate statistics based on the addresses or county of residence of sponsors for any visa applications. Therefore, it is not possible to provide figures requested.

question: 1349. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current Garda staffing levels at each Garda station across Longford-Westmeath; and the number of vacancies currently unfilled. [42316/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. I engage regularly with the Commissioner and I am assured that the resourcing of each Garda Division is fully considered within the overall context of the needs and requirements of Garda Divisions throughout the country. As Minister, my priority is getting more Gardaí into all our communities by supporting increased recruitment and appropriate civilianisation where possible. A Garda budget of €2.74 billion in 2026 will fund the recruitment of up to 1,000 new Gardaí, 200 more Garda staff and a doubling of the Garda Reserve to over 600. The Garda Commissioner and his senior management team keep the distribution of resources under ongoing review and I understand that, when allocating and transferring Garda members to and from any Division, consideration is given to commitments and undertakings outlined in the Annual Policing Plan. The Commissioner takes the requirements of all Garda Divisions nationwide into account, which include: • Local and national crime trends and workloads; • Policing arrangements and operational strategies; • Minimum establishment statistics; • Local population and trends, geographical area and size; • Transfer applications, including welfare, personnel issues and concerns. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Garda personnel nationally. This includes a breakdown of Garda Members and Staff assigned by Garda Station from 2010 to the end of April 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links: 2026 www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/garda-strength-breakdown-2026.html 2014-2025 www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html .

question: 1350. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of reported burglaries, thefts, and assaults recorded in counties Longford and Westmeath over the past five years; and the measures being taken to address rural crime concerns. [42317/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Central Statistics Office (CSO), as the national statistical agency, is responsible for the compilation and publication of crime statistics. The CSO produces these statistics using data recorded by An Garda Síochána on the PULSE system and publishes regular releases on recorded crime. The most recent release includes recorded crime up to the end of 2025. Crime statistics for a wide range of incident types, including “Burglaries and related offences”, “Theft and related offences”, "Assault causing harm" and "Assault other" are published annually, by Garda Division, on the CSO website and are available at the following link: www.data.cso.ie/table/CJQ06 . This Government is committed to building stronger, safer communities across the country. Rural crime covers a range of issues that cause concern for people living in rural communities, ranging from burglary and theft, to animal crime and road traffic offences. An Garda Síochána are committed to tackling all crime, including crime that occurs in our rural communities. Rural safety and community safety is not about policing alone of course – it requires a multi-agency, multi-sectoral and a whole-of-Government response. The Rural Safety Plan 2025-2027 brings together and strengthens all of the various strands of work being carried out in relation to rural safety. It has been developed by my Department, in conjunction with the National Rural Safety Forum. The Plan’s vision is to ensure people and communities in rural Ireland feel safe and are safe in their homes, places of work, and their local environments. It does this by identifying four key priority areas that we will focus on to achieve the overall goal. These areas are: Community Safety & Engagement, Property Crime, Roads Policing, and Animal & Wildlife Crime. A number of Garda operations are already supporting the plan, such as Operations Thor and Táirige, which tackle burglaries and thefts from homes, and retail crime respectively. Operation Thor actively targets organised crime groups through coordinated crime prevention and enforcement activity based on intelligence and the latest burglary trends. ‘Lock Up Light Up’ is An Garda Síochána's anti-burglary awareness campaign which encourages homeowners to protect their property from would-be criminals. In the 10 years since Operation Thor was introduced, burglary and related offences have significantly declined. Furthermore the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which I commenced in April 2025, provides for the establishment of Local Community Safety Partnerships within each local authority area. Safety Partnerships are independent, community-led bodies mandated to design tailored safety plans based on local priorities. They make their own decisions as to their day-to-day activity, operating in accordance with Statutory Regulations and having regard to Guidance from the National Office for Community Safety. Queries relating to their work should be directed to the relevant Safety Partnership. All 36 Local Community Safety Partnerships have now been established.

question: 1351. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the average waiting time for immigration and citizenship applications; and whether additional processing capacity is being provide (details supplied). [42318/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that my Department is in the process of implementing a modernisation programme for Immigration Service Delivery (ISD). The long-term strategic vision of ISD is to deliver a modern, transparent, and accessible immigration system - one that is faster, easier to navigate, and more efficient. In this context, the recent establishment of dedicated functions for Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing are intended to help streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving the service delivery for join family applications. My Department will be establishing further Case Processing functions later this year. My Department has also introduced a centralised Customer Engagement function, supported by a digital Customer Service Portal, to offer a modern customer contact centre to immigration applicants. The Customer Service Portal went live in October 2024, and is a self-service portal that enables applicants to check their immigration application status, book first-time registration appointments, and submit queries. The Customer Service Portal is now the primary avenue to communicate with my Department's immigration function which is committed to providing the best possible service to applicants. I can advise the Deputy that current visa processing times and decisions in the Dublin and Overseas Visa Offices are published on my Department's Immigration website here: www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/. The current processing times of applications for join family visas varies depending on the circumstances when the application is made. If a non-EEA national is moving to Ireland because they have been granted a Critical Skills Employment Permit they can apply for join family visas at the same time as their own employment visa. When these visas are applied for together, they are processed in tandem and are typically completed in under eight weeks. My Department aims to process join family visa applications made in other circumstances within 12 months. Applications to renew a permission in the state are managed by the Registration Office of ISD and processing times are updated every Monday and can be found here: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/ Applications for EU Treaty Rights Residence Cards under the Free Movement Directive, take on average 4-6 weeks to be acknowledged. A temporary permission is issued where appropriate at this stage. It can take up to six months to receive a decision on a Residence Card application. Applicants can also submit their application digitally on my Department's new online Case Processing system and can contact the processing team directly via this system. For naturalisation, most applicants can expect to receive a decision within one year. Citizenship applications made under S.16 "Irish Association" can take longer to process. With regards to international protection applications there has been a significant increase in investment into the international protection system over the last years which, combined with digitisation and process reengineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity and demonstrates a strong commitment to reducing cases on hand. To date in 2026, the median processing time for IPO first instance decisions is currently 12 months, with accelerated cases processed in 2 months, while standard cases are processed in 16 months. My Department continues to monitor processing times across all application streams.

question: 1353. Deputy Michael Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on the response to serious concerns regarding the impact of the Citywest IPAS accommodation centre (details supplied); the duty-of-care assessment that has been carried out for the existing local community and for businesses operating within the Citywest campus since the State acquired the complex; the Department, agency, centre operator, security provider, An Garda Síochána structure or other body that is accountable for responding to safety concerns both inside the campus grounds and in the surrounding village areas; the way in which he plans to ensure to ensure the safety of staff, customers, clients and visitors of premises operating within the Citywest campus grounds; the number of reported incidents, complaints or Garda notifications in the past 12 months involving public intoxication, drug use, aggressive behaviour, intimidation, antisocial behaviour or breaches of house rules, broken down between incidents within the Citywest IPAS centre, incidents within the wider Citywest campus grounds, and incidents reported in the surrounding local communities of Saggart, Rathcoole and Citywest; the current management escalation process for repeated breaches; if he will commit to open public engagement with residents and businesses rather than invitation-only meetings; the timeline for the promised Garda station; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42351/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The purchase of the Citywest property is a key part of the Government’s strategy to develop a stable and sustainable accommodation system for people seeking international protection by moving away from commercial properties to State-owned centres. The purchase of this site came with a strong commitment to engagement with the local community. There is an ongoing community engagement programme in place in Citywest, where officials from my department engage with representatives from the local community and local elected representatives to hear about and work to resolve local service matters that arise. The engagement process is co-designed with the Local Authority and implemented in collaboration with other local stakeholders, including the Local Development Company, South Dublin County Partnership. The engagement process ensures that we listen to the issues that have been identified at local level, to best support planning for essential supports and services that will assist with the integration process. A number of thematic issues and suggestions to strengthen public services and local infrastructure have been raised during these engagements, as have concerns about antisocial behaviour in the locality. Officials in my department and centre management continue to work very closely with An Garda Síochána in the area to keep all issues raised under review. The contracted accommodation provider at an International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centre is obliged to ensure provision of staffing and services at the centre. Security and supervision arrangements are provided for under the contract and include the need to comply with the licensing requirements of the Private Security Authority (PSA). The department is committed to ensuring that the local community has access to accurate information about this centre. Information is provided through the dedicated webpage www.gov.ie/citywest, direct contact with the Community Engagement Team through email and meetings with community stakeholders and the distribution of a leaflet to over 6,000 homes and businesses in the area around the centre, including Saggart and Rathcoole. When any incident occurs, IPAS teams engage with centre management to resolve the issue at hand. In this regard, the Department routinely engages with all providers in relation to incident response and policy compliance. Please see the following table updated to include statistics on incidents recorded in IPAS accommodation centres, dating back to 2021. Year Incidents Critical Incidents Warning Letters Transfers 2021 5 14 3 0 2022 766 37 659 110 2023 2,109 50 1,559 177 2024 4,168 55 3,170 521 2025 5,725 62 4,127 544 2026 to date 2,568 27 1,909 239 It should be noted when reviewing the statistics above that the number of people living in IPAS accommodation has increased very significantly over the last 5 years. Current resident numbers are approximately 33,000. Resident numbers at the end of 2021 were just over 7,000. Centre management in all IPAS centres have an ongoing working relationship with the local Gardaí. If there is ever any concern in relation to acts of violence or other criminal activity in any IPAS setting, An Garda Síochána are contacted. Data on operational actions by An Garda Síochána or convictions achieved against persons involved in threatening violent behaviour in IPAS centres is not collated by my department.

question: 1354. Deputy Mattie McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of fines issued arising from the operation of the GoSafe speed-detection van positioned on the Cashel Road in Clonmel, near the railway crossing, during the past 12 months; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42354/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Speeding remains one of the greatest risk factors on our roads. An Garda Síochána has contributed to making our roads safer through the use of mobile safety cameras, using service provider GoSafe to operate them on its behalf, enforcement cameras operated using a fleet of marked vehicles and static speed cameras. I am advised by the Garda authorities that from 1st May 2025 until 30th April 2026, there were 52 non-intercept (GoSafe detected) Fixed Charge Penalty Notices issued at the GoSafe site on the Cashel Road in Clonmel adjacent to the railway crossing. question: 1355. Deputy John Lahart asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current average processing times for Irish residence permit (IRP) renewals; the steps being taken to address ongoing delays and backlogs within immigration service delivery; whether he is considering the introduction of a further temporary extension to the validity of IRP cards in light of reported processing delays exceeding 12 weeks; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42372/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1305 and 1355 together. I understand the Deputy has clarified that his query relates to immigration permissions renewals and I can advise that the Registration Office of my Department is currently experiencing an exceptionally high demand for immigration permission renewal applications. I understand that the extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is exploring every avenue available to facilitate as many customers as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is open seven days a week to facilitate customers to process both first time registration appointments and online renewals. Additional staff have been assigned to this work, which has now begun to reduce the processing time for renewals. For certain categories of renewals, the processing time is now approximately 6 - 8 weeks from the time of initial application, with no category exceeding a wait time of 14 weeks. The Registration Office provide a live application processing date broken down by stamp category, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: [ ][ Renewing your registration permission if you live in the Republic of Ireland - Immigration Service Delivery ] (www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/). The Registration Office has also issued a notice to employers regarding the legality of employing someone awaiting renewal. This notice can be found here: [ ]www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/ If a person has any queries relating to their immigration permission or renewal, they can contact the registration office using my Departments Customer Service Portal. The Customer Service Portal can be accessed at the following link: [ www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ ] Details on how to submit a query to the registration office can be found at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/submitting-registration-or-renewal-queries/ . question: 1356. Deputy Michael Collins asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration given the implementation of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and the increasing long-term use of large-scale international protection accommodation centres, whether new operational standards or regulations will be introduced governing the management of such centres (details supplied), the interaction between centre management, residents and the local community and the provision of designated recreational and social spaces within centres; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42378/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The provision of supports and services to people seeking international protection is a whole of Government response. Residents of IPAS centres are provided with range of supports. This includes access to medical care via the HSE social inclusion outreach teams and medical card provision; IPAS customer services team clinics; onsite support from the provider’s staff; and psycho-social and integration support from NGO partners. IPAS has a dedicated Resident Welfare Team comprising subject matter experts seconded to the team on a full-time basis, as well as a number of support officers, who direct applicants with special reception needs within our accommodation, to relevant services or provide other appropriate information, as required. These include Social Workers and personnel from the National Social Inclusion Office at the HSE, Educational Welfare Officers (EWOs) from the Tusla Education Support Services (TESS). Where appropriate, the Resident Welfare Team engages with the centre managers and NGOs on-site to ensure that an applicant’s reception needs can be addressed within their current accommodation centre, providing information and support and signposting persons to relevant services. The Department's Community Engagement Team (CET) was established in late 2023 to engage directly with elected representatives, local authorities, An Garda Síochána, community members, and other service providers in advance of a new centre opening. In relation to larger State-owned sites, the model of engagement has been developed to plan for more meaningful dialogue to support these larger centres, particularly those on state-owned lands being developed under Government policy to move away from dependence on commercial providers. The CET team also links with other stakeholders outside of immediate openings of centres to build relationships and networks with key groups. This includes meetings with Community Integration Fora, Local Development Companies (LDCs) and other non-governmental organisations.

question: 1357. Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide clarity on the new guidelines for temporary protection supports for Ukrainians (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42405/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Minister O'Callaghan and I have received government approval for measures to transition Ukraine Accommodation Supports and Temporary Protection. The measures have been approved by government, in line with the EU Council recommendation for a co-ordinated approach to transition people out of Temporary Protection across the EU. Ireland intends to continue to support people from Ukraine who are beneficiaries of temporary protection. In recognition of the valuable contribution many people who have come from Ukraine since the outbreak of the war have made, Ireland will introduce an alternative permission to live and work here. This permission will be granted for a period of up to two years, renewable for periods of two years thereafter, with time on the permission counting towards naturalisation. Eligibility criteria will apply, including a requirement to be earning a minimum of €29,432 per year. More information on these criteria can be found at [ Ukraine Updates (EN) ] (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/). An applicant must demonstrate that they have been in employment or self-employment for a period of six months prior to the application and demonstrate that they will earn an annual gross salary of €29,432. Persons who are unable to satisfy the eligibility criteria will continue to be entitled to Temporary Protection Status while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect. While temporary protection is in place until March 2027, there may be further extensions to the directive which will be agreed at EU level. As mentioned above, beneficiaries of temporary protection will remain entitled to this protection while the Directive is in effect.

question: 1360. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of deaths that occurred in direct provision for each of the past 20 years; and the ages of those who passed while in direct provision. [42481/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Any death of a resident in International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) accommodation is a tragic event for their family, friends and neighbours, and also for the accommodation centre staff who know them. The Department publishes information on deaths of people staying in IPAS centres at: www.gov.ie/en/international-protection-accommodation-services-ipas/publications/statistics-on-deaths-of-international-protection-accommodation-service-residents/, with the most recent publication reporting on the period to January-December 2025. The data provided show that 23 IPAS residents died in 2025. 15 IPAS residents died in 2024, and this compares to 9 in 2023. It is relevant to note that from 2023 to 2024, the number of people resident in IPAS increased by more than 25%. The statistical breakdown of deaths and information on cause of death is grouped to protect the identity of the people concerned and their families. Where the cause of death is not publicly available or has not been confirmed by the General Registration Office (GRO), it is noted as “Not Available”. The Department does not have any input into the process of reporting or recording of deaths by the GRO. This publication is in line with the Department's policy on 'Recording & Reporting of Deaths of Residents in International Protection and Accommodation Centres’, a copy of which is published at: www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/policy-on-the-recording-reporting-of-deaths-of-residents-in-international-protection-a.pdf

question: 1362. Deputy Fionntán Ó Súilleabháin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of asylum applications made at the immigration office in Dublin city centre compared with those at the airports and seaports in each of the past five years, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42541/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am fully committed to ensuring that Ireland’s International Protection system is robust, and rules based, and that our borders are protected. The State is required to examine the application of anyone who presents at the borders of the State, or is in the State, and indicates that they wish to make an application for international protection. This is in accordance with our obligations under international and EU asylum law and the Government takes those commitments very seriously. There are a number of circumstances where a person might apply at the International Protection Office (IPO) without first applying at a port of entry. They may enter at an airport with valid documentation for example but choose not to apply at that time. Or they may apply having been in the State for a period previously, for example on foot of a different permission to remain. question: 1363. Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the costs of all deportation charter flights to date; the cost of each flight; the number of deportees on board; and if he is examining ways to reduce the cost involved. [42547/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based. The enforcement aspects of our laws, including deportation orders, are an essential requirement for the system to work effectively and to ensure that there is confidence in the application of our legislation in this area. Deportations are costly and complex to enforce. It is the preferred option to return people voluntarily and my Department has a voluntary return programme to assist people to return prior to the issuance of a deportation order. A person can only avail of voluntary return before a deportation order is issued and I have increased resources into this programme to enable individuals who wish to return before a deportation order is issued to them. A deportation order is a legal order to leave the State. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed. My Department works closely with the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) to progress arrangements for the removal of people subject to deportation orders. The number of deportation orders signed in 2024 (2,403) increased by 180% compared to 2023 (857). In 2025, 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared to 2024. 2,108 deportation orders have been signed up to 5 June 2026. In 2024, 1,122 people departed from the State under various mechanisms (i.e. enforced deportation, voluntary return etc.). In 2025, 2,111 people had their departure confirmed through these pathways, an increase of 88% compared to 2024. Up to 5 June 2026, 977 people have departed the State through these pathways. In 2025, six charter flight operations removed 205 people from the State. Of these, five operations to non-EU destinations removed 182 people who were subject to deportation orders and one operation removed 23 EU citizens on grounds of criminality. Three charter operations to date in 2026 have seen the removal of 130 people from the State, including 67 EU citizens who were removed on grounds of criminality. Charter flight services are provided by Air Partner Ltd under a contract entered into in November 2024. This contract was signed following a competitive and open procurement process. The potential value of this contract is €5m over the lifespan of the contract. The term of the contract is 3 years with a possibility to extend it twice by one year, a potential lifespan of 5 years in total. The total expenditure under the contract with Air Partner will be based on the number of charter flights provided, the frequency of which will be determined by the operational needs of the State. Charter flights provide an alternative to commercial flights and can be more appropriate in circumstances when a group of individuals are being removed to the same destination. This has increased the options available to An Garda Síochána to effect removals and deportations. The table below sets out the provisional costs for the nine charter flights that have occurred under this contract to date. Date Destination Number of people removed Cost (excl. VAT) 27/02/2025 Georgia (one way) 32 €102,476 01/05/2025 Georgia (one way) 39 €103,751 04/06/2026 Nigeria (return) 35 €324,714 23/09/2025 Pakistan (return) 24 €473,000 13/10/2025 Romania (one way) 23 €69,475 03/11/2025 Georgia (return) 52 €187,625 25/01/2026 Poland/Lithuania (return) 33 €122,660 28/02/2026 South Africa (return) 63 €585,075 24/05/2026 Poland/Lithuania (return) 34 €184,465 A number of factors impact the costs associated with deportation operations. In particular, the costs for any particular deportation reflect the numbers travelling in each instance, the destination country, and if direct flights are not available the escorts and deportee transit through a hub airport.

question: 1364. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when his Department will take over management and operations of a facility (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42579/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1364 to 1366, inclusive, together. The purchase of the Citywest property is a key part of the Government’s strategy to develop a stable and sustainable accommodation system for people seeking international protection by moving away from commercial properties to State-owned centres. The Citywest has been successfully used as a processing centre and accommodation centre since 2022, with registration services provided to both people applying for Temporary Protection due to war in Ukraine, and to people applying for international protection. The former Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre have been in State ownership since August 2025. The department contracts a service provider on its behalf to provide services on site. The Department has been responsible for management and oversight of all International Protection and Temporary Protection services provided on the campus at all times since services commenced in 2022. The Citywest facility is a key component in the State's implementation of the EU Migration Pact this year, acting as a screening centre and border procedure location as required under the Pact. The new International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and was passed into law last month. The new rules will take effect on 12 June 2026, later this week. Reforming and speeding up processing of applications should also serve over time to reduce the scale of the demand for international protection accommodation. A new State body will have responsibility for appeals, and our removal and deportations process will be faster and less bureaucratic. Ultimately, improved, faster processing will result in decreasing annual costs by reducing the time an applicant remains in the system. Faster processing under the Pact will mean that applicants spend less time in IPAS accommodation, and this will significantly reduce the cost of the asylum system to the State. The purchase of this site came with a strong commitment to engagement with the local community. A community engagement process was initiated following the Government’s approval to purchase the former Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre for the provision of accommodation for people seeking international protection. The engagement process is co-designed with the Local Authority and implemented in collaboration with other local stakeholders, including the Local Development Company, South Dublin County Partnership. The engagement process ensures that we listen to the issues that have been identified at local level, to best support planning for essential supports and services that will assist with the integration process. Information is provided through the dedicated webpage, www.gov.ie/citywest, direct contact with the Community Engagement Team (CET) through email, regular meetings with community stakeholders and the distribution of a leaflet to over 6,000 homes and businesses in the area around the centre, including Saggart and Rathcoole. A number of thematic issues and suggestions to strengthen public services and local infrastructure have been raised during engagements with community stakeholders and elected representatives. Suggestions will be considered in the context of the Government's commitment to listening to local people and leaders and helping to support the delivery of services in the area.
