question: 1366. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to give an update on the plans for a facility (details supplied) to transition to a processing centre; when this will happen; to outline what this will mean for the facility; the processing times expected per person; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42581/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1364 to 1366, inclusive, together. The purchase of the Citywest property is a key part of the Government’s strategy to develop a stable and sustainable accommodation system for people seeking international protection by moving away from commercial properties to State-owned centres. The Citywest has been successfully used as a processing centre and accommodation centre since 2022, with registration services provided to both people applying for Temporary Protection due to war in Ukraine, and to people applying for international protection. The former Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre have been in State ownership since August 2025. The department contracts a service provider on its behalf to provide services on site. The Department has been responsible for management and oversight of all International Protection and Temporary Protection services provided on the campus at all times since services commenced in 2022. The Citywest facility is a key component in the State's implementation of the EU Migration Pact this year, acting as a screening centre and border procedure location as required under the Pact. The new International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and was passed into law last month. The new rules will take effect on 12 June 2026, later this week. Reforming and speeding up processing of applications should also serve over time to reduce the scale of the demand for international protection accommodation. A new State body will have responsibility for appeals, and our removal and deportations process will be faster and less bureaucratic. Ultimately, improved, faster processing will result in decreasing annual costs by reducing the time an applicant remains in the system. Faster processing under the Pact will mean that applicants spend less time in IPAS accommodation, and this will significantly reduce the cost of the asylum system to the State. The purchase of this site came with a strong commitment to engagement with the local community. A community engagement process was initiated following the Government’s approval to purchase the former Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre for the provision of accommodation for people seeking international protection. The engagement process is co-designed with the Local Authority and implemented in collaboration with other local stakeholders, including the Local Development Company, South Dublin County Partnership. The engagement process ensures that we listen to the issues that have been identified at local level, to best support planning for essential supports and services that will assist with the integration process. Information is provided through the dedicated webpage, www.gov.ie/citywest, direct contact with the Community Engagement Team (CET) through email, regular meetings with community stakeholders and the distribution of a leaflet to over 6,000 homes and businesses in the area around the centre, including Saggart and Rathcoole. A number of thematic issues and suggestions to strengthen public services and local infrastructure have been raised during engagements with community stakeholders and elected representatives. Suggestions will be considered in the context of the Government's commitment to listening to local people and leaders and helping to support the delivery of services in the area.

question: 1367. Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to the publishing of the new 2025 Irish Association guidelines, the number of section 16 Irish Association applicants who were approved for citizenship having zero years residency, one-year residency, two-year residency, three-year residency, four-year residency and five-year residency in the State, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42590/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1367 and 1374 together. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually in accordance with the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/ I can inform the Deputy that it is not possible to provide statistics on the number of applications approved or refused under Section 16 based on residency in the State, or based on any particular criterion or combination of criteria contained in the Irish Association guidelines. This would require the manual examination of hundreds of cases. Such an examination would require a disproportionate amount of time and resources. I can advise the Deputy that the overall number of decisions issued on the Irish Association applications since the introduction of the Guidelines in April 2025 is 382, of which 243 were refusals.

question: 1368. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether any review has been conducted into the causes of exceptionally high waiting times for domestic violence applications in certain District Court offices, including Naas, Sligo, Castlebar and Galway; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42609/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Management of the courts is the responsibility of the Courts Service, which is independent in exercising its functions under the Courts Service Act 1998 and the Constitution. Logistical and operational matters are matters for the Courts Service. Furthermore, the scheduling of court cases and the allocation of court business is a matter for the Presidents of the Courts and the presiding judges who are, under the Constitution, independent in the exercise of their judicial functions. To be of assistance, I have referred the Deputy's question to the Courts Service for direct reply.

question: 1369. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether additional sitting days, judicial resources or administrative staffing have been allocated since 2024 to District Court offices experiencing extended waiting times for domestic violence applications; and if they will provide details by court district. [42610/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As Minister, it is my priority to ensure that the courts are resourced to administer justice efficiently and effectively. In relation to steps taken to increase the number of judges, to ensure that our judiciary is resourced appropriately, 24 additional judges were appointed in 2023 on foot of the Judicial Planning Working Group report. On December 10 2025, the Courts and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2025 was signed into law by the President, and the relevant provisions to allow for the recruitment of additional judges were commenced on 30 January 2026. The Act provides for the increase in the number of judges in each Court jurisdiction by a further 21 posts. Taken together, these two sets of appointments represent an increase of approximately 25% in the number of Judges in Ireland. Under the Courts Service Act 1998, the management and administration of the courts is a matter for the Courts Service, while the allocation of court business, the scheduling of cases and the management of court lists are matters for the Judiciary, in particular the Presidents of the Courts. Judges are, under the Constitution and the law, independent in the exercise of their judicial functions. I am advised by the Courts Service that it does not hold the information sought, in the format requested, on the allocation of additional sittings, judicial resources or administrative staffing in respect of domestic violence applications, as resources are assigned to court offices and court areas to support a range of business, including crime, civil and family matters, rather than being allocated by reference to domestic violence applications only. I am further informed by the Courts Service that waiting times for domestic violence applications (and all other District Court business) are kept under review by the President of the District Court as part of the ongoing management of court business. The Courts Service works closely with the Judiciary to support the efficient operation of the courts and to minimise delays, including facilitating additional sittings where this is possible within available resources.

question: 1370. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has assessed whether delays in substantive domestic violence proceedings may increase risks to applicants, including repeat incidents or breaches requiring Garda intervention; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42613/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The management of court proceedings are matters for the Courts Service and the independent judiciary. Where breaches of court orders or alleged criminal offences arise, these are matters for investigation by An Garda Síochána, who are operationally independent in the exercise of their functions. My Department has not conducted a specific review of the nature outlined by the Deputy. I am, however, conscious of the impact that delays in courts proceedings can have on those involved in domestic violence cases, which can prolong uncertainty for applicants and can be distressing for all parties concerned. Supporting and protecting victims is a key priority for my Department. This commitment is underpinned by the Government’s Zero Tolerance Third National Strategy on Domestic, Sexual and Gender Based Violence, which sets out a comprehensive whole of Government approach to preventing DSGBV, supporting victims, and strengthening the criminal justice response. I am also committed to ensuring the effective operation of the family justice system. On 22 April 2026, I published the Implementation Plan for the Family Courts Act 2024. The Plan will result in some of the most significant reforms of the family justice system in the history of the state. The Family Courts Act 2024 contains a number of provisions designed to make the family court process a more efficient, accessible and user focused system, including through improved case management and measures designed to reduce delays. The ongoing Modernisation Programme for the Courts Service, including the digitalisation of procedures, will also assist in improving the efficiency and timeliness of processing cases.

question: 1371. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he intends to review the process through which children of Irish citizens who were born in another country can become Irish citizens; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42627/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that any person born outside the island of Ireland can become an Irish citizen if one of their parents was an Irish citizen at the time of their birth or through an Irish national grandparent born in Ireland. A person can also obtain Irish citizenship through the Foreign Births Register, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is responsible for the operation of the Register. For more information please see: www.dfa.ie/citizenship/born-abroad/registering-a-foreign-birth/ I have no plans at this time to review the process through which children of Irish citizens born abroad can become Irish citizens.

question: 1372. Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of vehicles seized for having no insurance within Galway division in 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form. [42641/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational policing matters. Road traffic legislation is enforced as part of the day-to-day duties of members of An Garda Síochána, as well as through a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies, in order to make our roads safer for all. I am informed by Garda authorities that there were 1,066 incidents in which a vehicle was detained by Garda authorities in Galway division for having no insurance in 2025 and 364 as of 31 May 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. Vehicles seized or detained relate to those detained under s41 of the Road Traffic Act. In the interest of transparency, An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to figures relating to Roads Policing Offences and Activity nationwide. This can be found at the following link:www.garda.ie/en/roads-policing/statistics/roads%20policing%20offences%20by%20region%20and%20division

question: 1373. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on a probate case (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42656/26]

question: 1375. Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the immigration or residence permission planned for elderly Ukrainians under temporary protection after March, 2027; to outline whether humanitarian circumstances such as age, widowhood, dependency on family members in Ireland, and long established family ties will be taken into account; whether people in these circumstances may qualify for a longer-term permission such as stamp four; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42732/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice On 26 May 2026 Government approved measures to support those displaced by the war in Ukraine to transition from Temporary Protection status in line with the EU Council recommendation for a co-ordinated approach to transition people out of Temporary Protection across the EU. Ireland intends to continue to support people fleeing the war in Ukraine who are Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection. In recognition of the valuable contribution many people who have come from Ukraine since the outbreak of the war have made, Ireland will introduce an alternative permission to live and work here. This permission will be granted for a period of up to two years, renewable for periods of two years thereafter, with time on the permission counting towards naturalisation. Eligibility criteria will apply. More information on these criteria can be found at Ukraine Updates (EN) (www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/campaigns/ukraine-updates-en/). Persons who do not meet the eligibility criteria for this permission will remain entitled to Temporary Protection while the Temporary Protection Directive is in effect. The Directive is currently in place until March 2027 and there may be further extensions to the Directive which will be agreed at EU level. Ongoing supports for people with particular circumstances that would make it difficult for them to manage in independent accommodation will be provided. Coordinated work between my department, Irish Red Cross, the International Organisation for Migration and other relevant stakeholders will ensure that individuals can make decisions about their future options in Ireland with as much clarity as possible.

question: 1377. Deputy Niamh Smyth asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to three commissioned houses (detail supplied) that are ready to go but no social workers have been appointed to make them functional; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42752/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Cuan, the statutory domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) agency is committed to providing safe and accessible accommodation and support services for victims and survivors of DSGBV. I am informed that Cuan is actively engaging with key stakeholders including Safe Ireland, the lead Approved Housing Body, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, Cavan and Monaghan County Councils and the Housing Agency, to progress the development of a 12-unit refuge in this region, which will also include community-facing ancillary support services, thereby strengthening domestic violence support in the region. I am advised that Cuan is also currently considering future options for potential refuge provision in Cavan, in parallel with progression of the refuge site identified in Monaghan. Both Cavan County Council and Monaghan County Council have committed the allocation of three units from their social housing stock which will deliver an additional six safe homes across the region. Cuan is working with Safe Ireland to finalise operational and staffing costs. Recruitment is underway for the staff associated with these safe homes. All six units will become operational in 2026. Safe Ireland is working with the stakeholder group to create a solid infrastructure and a coherent connected response across both counties. Cuan has agreed to allocate additional resources to Safe Ireland. These additional resources will support Safe Ireland in its capacity to expand its services to provide both emergency refuge and safe home accommodation in the Cavan/Monaghan region.

question: 1378. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the Government intends to publish a Retail Crime Strategy; the timeline for its publication; the measures that will be included to reduce retail crime and support affected businesses; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42831/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1378, 1379, 1380, 1381, 1382, 1383, 1384 and 1385 together. This Government takes any risk to retailers and retail staff very seriously. I am acutely aware of the personal and economic impact that retail crime is having on businesses, retail workers and communities. I recognise that shoplifting and organised retail crime pose a significant threat to the economic welfare of Irish retailers and that retail theft is not a victimless crime. The Programme for Government makes a number of commitments relating to retail crime, many of which will be dealt with in the context of the Retail Crime Strategy, which is also a commitment under the Programme. These include: • Support Garda Operations to tackle retail crime including through the use of organised crime and proceeds of crime legislation; • Examine the introduction of a specific offence of assaulting a retail worker; • Tackle the practice of “retail defamation”; • Improve data sharing between retailers and Gardaí; • Expand the use of community sanctions for retail crime; • Update the Public Order Acts to allow a prolific offender to be excluded from a retail premises for a certain period of time. Work on the Strategy is well advanced and I expect to receive a draft in the coming weeks for detailed consideration. I look forward to engaging with its proposed objectives, priorities and recommendations to ensure that the final Strategy reflects the priorities of the Government and the needs of retailers, workers and communities. Following this process and subject to final approval, it is my intention to publish the Strategy later this year. Furthermore it should be noted that my Department’s work in relation to community safety, youth justice interventions and antisocial behaviour, as well as securing funding for more Garda recruitment for high visibility policing, will also contribute to the aim of supporting retailers, their staff and their customers. Supports for retailers affected by retail crime falls under the Department for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. The Department of Enterprise holds a Retail Forum on a quarterly basis with retailers and representative bodies, hosted by the Minister of State with responsibility for Small Businesses and Retail. This provides an opportunity to discuss key issues of importance with key stakeholders in the sector.

Furthermore it should be noted that my Department’s work in relation to community safety, youth justice interventions and antisocial behaviour, as well as securing funding for more Garda recruitment for high visibility policing, will also contribute to the aim of supporting retailers, their staff and their customers. Supports for retailers affected by retail crime falls under the Department for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. The Department of Enterprise holds a Retail Forum on a quarterly basis with retailers and representative bodies, hosted by the Minister of State with responsibility for Small Businesses and Retail. This provides an opportunity to discuss key issues of importance with key stakeholders in the sector.

question: 1385. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department is examining measures to address the practice commonly referred to as retail defamation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42838/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1378, 1379, 1380, 1381, 1382, 1383, 1384 and 1385 together. This Government takes any risk to retailers and retail staff very seriously. I am acutely aware of the personal and economic impact that retail crime is having on businesses, retail workers and communities. I recognise that shoplifting and organised retail crime pose a significant threat to the economic welfare of Irish retailers and that retail theft is not a victimless crime. The Programme for Government makes a number of commitments relating to retail crime, many of which will be dealt with in the context of the Retail Crime Strategy, which is also a commitment under the Programme. These include: • Support Garda Operations to tackle retail crime including through the use of organised crime and proceeds of crime legislation; • Examine the introduction of a specific offence of assaulting a retail worker; • Tackle the practice of “retail defamation”; • Improve data sharing between retailers and Gardaí; • Expand the use of community sanctions for retail crime; • Update the Public Order Acts to allow a prolific offender to be excluded from a retail premises for a certain period of time. Work on the Strategy is well advanced and I expect to receive a draft in the coming weeks for detailed consideration. I look forward to engaging with its proposed objectives, priorities and recommendations to ensure that the final Strategy reflects the priorities of the Government and the needs of retailers, workers and communities. Following this process and subject to final approval, it is my intention to publish the Strategy later this year. Furthermore it should be noted that my Department’s work in relation to community safety, youth justice interventions and antisocial behaviour, as well as securing funding for more Garda recruitment for high visibility policing, will also contribute to the aim of supporting retailers, their staff and their customers. Supports for retailers affected by retail crime falls under the Department for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. The Department of Enterprise holds a Retail Forum on a quarterly basis with retailers and representative bodies, hosted by the Minister of State with responsibility for Small Businesses and Retail. This provides an opportunity to discuss key issues of importance with key stakeholders in the sector.

question: 1386. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to expand on the role of IPAS resident welfare services; the funding provided to the service by his Department in 2021 to 2025, and to date in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42896/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) has a Resident Welfare Team which was established to support IPAS to meet its obligations under the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. 230 of 2018) and it continues to do this in adherence with the International Protection Act 2026. The Resident Welfare Team are part of the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration's core staff. It is a multi-disciplinary team supporting international protection applicants resident in IPAS accommodation centres, in particular those with vulnerabilities and complex needs. It comprises Social Work Advisors (some of which are appointed Child and Adult Safeguarding Leads) and Educational Welfare Officers from the TUSLA Education Support Services, in addition to a team of civil servants. The team also engages with dedicated liaison personnel from the National Social Inclusion Office in the HSE. The provision of supports and services to people seeking international protection is a whole of Government response and the Resident Welfare Team liaises with various Government departments in this regard. The team and the stakeholders listed above engage with applicants with special reception needs resident in IPAS accommodation, to signpost them to relevant services, supports and provide other appropriate information, as required. The Resident Welfare Team engages with centre managers and NGOs at centres to ensure that an applicant’s reception needs can be addressed within their accommodation centre. Where required, the Resident Welfare Team engages to assist with transfers to alternative accommodation.

question: 1387. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has a formal working agreement or contract with any NGO operating in the international protection advocacy space; if so, the costs associated with same from 2021 to date; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42897/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I regret it has not been possible to collate the information requested by the Deputy in the time available. I will write to the Deputy directly once the information is to hand.

question: 1388. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his views on correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42898/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1388 and 1405 together. Legal migration plays an essential and positive role in Ireland's society, as immigrants bring essential skills and experience that are much needed in the current labour market and are vital to addressing labour shortages. I am fully committed to ensuring that Ireland’s International Protection and immigration systems are robust, rules based and that the integrity of all our processes is maintained at all times. As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act was passed into law last month and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. My Department continues to focus on preparing for these new rules to take effect on 12 June 2026. The Pact will provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures and two months for processing applicants who have applied for protection elsewhere in Europe. Faster processing will mean that applicants spend less time in International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS) accommodation, and this will significantly reduce the cost of the asylum system to the State. Faster decision-making will also mean that successful applicants will be granted international protection sooner, and those whose applications are refused can be returned to their country of origin sooner. The enforcement aspects of our laws, including deportation orders, are an essential requirement for the system to work effectively and to ensure that there is confidence in the application of our legislation in this area. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed, and my Department has taken action to significantly improve immigration enforcement measures and increase removals. The number of deportation orders signed has increased in recent years. In 2024 (2,403) the number of orders signed increased by 180% compared to 2023 (857). In 2025, 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared to 2024. 2,108 deportation orders have been signed up to 05 June 2026. In 2024, 1,122 people departed from the State under various mechanisms (i.e. enforced deportation, voluntary return etc.). In 2025, 2,111 people had their departure confirmed through these pathways, an increase of 88% compared to 2024. Up to 05 June 2026, 977 people have departed the State through these pathways. The Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy detailing how Government intends to meet the demands, opportunities, and challenges facing Ireland’s society and economy over the next decade. My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of other Government departments to develop this strategy with the aim to publish Ireland’s first overarching whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy later this year. The scope of the Strategy will include issues such as labour market needs, legal pathways, international education and planning for public service provision including housing, amongst other issues relating to migration. To that end, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024 to support that work which now consists of ten Government Departments meeting at senior official level. The key objective of the Strategy and the SMPG is to develop a whole-of-government approach to migration policy that is coherent across Departments and responsive in seeking to address Ireland’s current and future demographic, economic and social policy needs. More broadly, capacity-based planning for Government services is a matter for each Department in its area of responsibility, be that Health, Education, Housing or any other sector, whether the demand for those services increases or declines in line with demographic changes, and whether those demographic changes arise from natural increases or declines in population or from immigration or emigration. The Government considers such matters at a central level in initiatives such as the National Development Plan and National Planning Framework, and via consideration at appropriate Cabinet Committees of capacity planning measures.

question: 1389. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of administrative staff in the Clare/Tipperary Garda division overall; the number of administrative staff in the Clare portion of the aforementioned Garda division; a breakdown of which stations they are based in; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42899/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. I am assured that the resourcing of each Garda Division is fully considered within the overall context of the needs and requirements of Garda Divisions throughout the country. For the Deputy’s information, An Garda Síochána publish information in relation to An Garda Síochána staff by Division and Station which is publicly available and can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/garda-statistics/human%20resources/ The Deputy should select the statistics for 2026, the most recent available date and then select the file titled ‘Garda Staff by Division and Station" to access a breakdown of administrative staff assigned to the Clare/Tipperary Division and a breakdown of staff assigned to each station in County Clare. As Minister, I am fully committed to ensuring that An Garda Síochána has the resources it needs. As part of Budget 2026 I provided an unprecedented €2.74 billion to support recruitment, training and staffing. This will support recruitment of up to 1,000 Gardai, 200 more Garda staff and additional members of the Garda Reserve. Garda Staff are an integral part of our police service and they are involved in the provision of a wide range of administrative, professional and technical services. As well as providing clerical support and financial management functions in Garda stations and offices across the country, Garda Staff carry out a range of specialised support roles. In recent years, these additional staff have provided expertise in support of the investigation of crime and freed up 900 Gardaí for deployment to frontline duties.

question: 1390. Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the eligibility rules and regulatory framework governing access to full-time further education and training , such as post leaving certificate courses for those holding stamp one-g or stamp three immigration permissions; if individuals with these stamps are permitted to enrol in full-time academic courses; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [42911/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that Stamp 1G and Stamp 3 immigration permissions do not prevent the holder from engaging in study, however, there are different conditions associated with each permission. Apart from the Third Level Graduate Programme, a Stamp 1G may be granted to spouses, de facto partners or children of Critical Skills Employment Permit, General Employment Permit or Intra-Company Transfer Employment Permit holders, or researchers on a Hosting Agreement. A Stamp 3 immigration permission is granted to people in the State as Ministers of Religion and volunteers working with charitable organisations, as well as spouses, de facto partners and children of certain non-EEA nationals. Individuals on a Stamp 1G or Stamp 3 immigration permission can enrol on, and commence any course listed on the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP), or eligible programmes offered by providers with authorisation to use the new TrustEd Education mark awarded by the Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI), be that an English language course or a third level degree course. The eligibility rules and regulatory framework governing access to full-time further education and training are a matter for the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.

question: 1391. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a building is still in his Department's use (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43007/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Department can confirm that the property listed in the detail supplied is currently in use as an International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centre. Where a contract or a property is providing services within its obligations and can be seen as delivering value for State funds, it is important to maintain our ability to meet need across the system. While numbers of people applying for international protection have reduced, there have been approximately 1,000 applications per month since early 2026, and accommodation remains an essential need. My Department is working to increase the amount of State-owned international protection accommodation and creating a more stable and sustainable accommodation system. As developing these more sustainable State-owned accommodation system options under this strategy will take time, the commissioning of emergency commercial accommodation will continue to be a feature in the short to medium term.

question: 1392. Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of the application for funding under the IIP scheme for the redevelopment and upgrade of a location (details supplied); the expected timeline for a decision on this application; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43019/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As Minister, I do not comment on individual Immigrant Investor Programme (IIP) applications. My Department is committed to ensuring that all applications will be examined on their own merits and will endeavour to conclude all decisions in a timely manner. If a project owner has any queries, they can contact the IIP Unit of my Department directly.

question: 1393. Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of minibuses currently operational per Garda station for community policing in the Dublin metropolitan region, in tabular form; if there is funding for additional minibuses for the DMR to apply for; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43036/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which includes all operational policing matters, such as the distribution and deployment of the Garda fleet across the State. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. I am informed by the Garda authorities that, as of 31 May 2026, there were 3,762 vehicles attached to the Garda fleet. An Garda Síochána have advised that minibuses are managed as Divisional resources and may be utilised across multiple Garda stations within a Division. For that reason, the Garda authorities have advised that a Divisional summary provides a more accurate basis for reporting than a station-by-station breakdown. The Garda authorities have provided the table below which sets out the number of minibuses allocated to Community Policing in the Dublin Metropolitan Region, as of 29 May 2026. DMR Allocated East 1 North 0 North Central 1 South 1 South Central 3 West 1 Total 7 The purchase and allocation of vehicles by An Garda Síochána is made on the basis of identified operational demands, the availability of resources, and is reviewed on a continual basis.

question: 1394. Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when individuals eligible for the ex-gratia Stardust victims recognition payment scheme will receive payment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43054/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration On 16 February last, I announced the details the Stardust Recognition Payment Scheme. The scheme is available to all survivor beneficiaries of the original Stardust Victims Compensation Tribunal established in 1985. The Stardust Recognition Scheme can be accessed online at www.stardustrecognitionpayment.ie and applications can be made online or by post. A Stardust Recognition Payment Helpline has also been set up that is be available during office hours, for those who wish to request an application form to be sent to their home address. Since the Stardust Recognition Payment Scheme opened in February this year, over 450 people have applied. The Scheme will be open for applications until 5pm on 17 August 2026. Completed applications are reviewed by the Stardust Recognition Payment Unit for completeness. In making an application, applicants consent to providing any relevant information requested by the Stardust Recognition Payment Unit that is required to validate their application. Once all criteria are met, the applicant is then contacted to finalise arrangements and information for payment. It is expected that the first payments will be processed in the coming weeks.

question: 1395. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the join family visa application (details supplied); a timeline for its processing; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43064/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that the Join Family visa application referred to was created on 19 March 2025. Supporting documentation was received in the Warsaw office on 24 March 2025. The application was received in the Dublin Visa Office on 09 April 2025 where it awaits examination and processing. My Department's business target for join family visa applications is 12 months. It must be made clear that these are business targets for the immigration service and some applications can take longer than others. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification. While I acknowledge the personal difficulties an applicant might be experiencing; it is not possible to give a definitive date as to when this application will be finalised. All applications are processed in chronological order, based on date order of receipt. While every effort is made to process applications as soon as possible, processing times will vary having regard to the volume and complexity of applications, the possible need for the Immigration Service Delivery function of my Department to investigate, inquire into, or seek further information, and the resources available. The current processing times for Dublin visa decisions is available here: (www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/) . The date published on the website is the oldest date of application currently being processed under a given category. However, it should be noted that the Visa team continue to process and make decisions on applications received after the published processing date. If a particular application takes longer to consider this may result in the published processing date remaining unchanged. I can assure you that this does not indicate the processing of these applications has halted overall. I am acutely aware that join family applications are very important for the people impacted. I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland, and I am committed to improving the service my Department provides. The person concerned can now directly check the status of their visa application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: (www.portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/) . As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 1396. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the longest processing time for a join family visa for 2025 and to date in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43066/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1396, 1397, 1398, 1399, 1400, 1401, 1402 and 1403 together. I can advise the Deputy that on 26 November 2025, Minister O'Callaghan and I published the review of the non-EEA Family Reunification Policy, which has remained largely unchanged since 2013, and sets out how Irish citizens and most non-EEA Irish residents may apply to bring non-EEA family members to live with them in Ireland. The revised Policy includes a number of changes, the majority of which took effect for new applications from 26 November, with longer term measures to be introduced as soon as operational considerations allow. The revised policy can be accessed on my Department’s website at the following link: (www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/f88cb36e/Revised_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf). Applications made before 26 November 2025 are assessed under the previous policy, which is available at the following link: (www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Policy-document-on-Non-EEA-family-reunification.pdf) . I can advise the Deputy that my Department currently operates seven overseas Visa Offices in addition to the Visa Office in Dublin. These are located in Abuja, Beijing, London, Moscow, Ankara, Abu Dhabi and New Delhi. In addition, staff of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade process certain visa applications in Irish Embassies abroad under delegated authority from my Department. The current processing times of applications for join family visas varies depending on the circumstances when the application is made. If a non-EEA national is moving to Ireland because they have been granted a Critical Skills Employment Permit they can apply for join family visas at the same time as their own employment visa. When these visas are applied for together, they are processed in tandem and are typically completed in under eight weeks. My Department aims to process join family visa applications made in other circumstances within 12 months. I can assure the Deputy the majority of join family visas receive a first instance decision within the 12 month business target. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification. In 2025 the average processing time for all types of Join Family visa applications was 113 days. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I want to assure anyone who has made an application for a visa that my Department is doing everything possible to progress these applications as quickly as possible. In this context, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated teams for Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing are intended to help streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving the service delivery for join family visa applications. Processing times and decisions at the Dublin Visa Office and the Overseas Visa Offices can be checked at the following link: https://www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/ My Department does not compile statistics in a manner which would identify individual applications as having been processed in the longest or shortest time period. question: 1398. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the process behind the assessment and approval of a join family visa; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43068/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1396, 1397, 1398, 1399, 1400, 1401, 1402 and 1403 together. I can advise the Deputy that on 26 November 2025, Minister O'Callaghan and I published the review of the non-EEA Family Reunification Policy, which has remained largely unchanged since 2013, and sets out how Irish citizens and most non-EEA Irish residents may apply to bring non-EEA family members to live with them in Ireland. The revised Policy includes a number of changes, the majority of which took effect for new applications from 26 November, with longer term measures to be introduced as soon as operational considerations allow. The revised policy can be accessed on my Department’s website at the following link: (www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/f88cb36e/Revised_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf). Applications made before 26 November 2025 are assessed under the previous policy, which is available at the following link: (www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Policy-document-on-Non-EEA-family-reunification.pdf) . I can advise the Deputy that my Department currently operates seven overseas Visa Offices in addition to the Visa Office in Dublin. These are located in Abuja, Beijing, London, Moscow, Ankara, Abu Dhabi and New Delhi. In addition, staff of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade process certain visa applications in Irish Embassies abroad under delegated authority from my Department. The current processing times of applications for join family visas varies depending on the circumstances when the application is made. If a non-EEA national is moving to Ireland because they have been granted a Critical Skills Employment Permit they can apply for join family visas at the same time as their own employment visa. When these visas are applied for together, they are processed in tandem and are typically completed in under eight weeks. My Department aims to process join family visa applications made in other circumstances within 12 months. I can assure the Deputy the majority of join family visas receive a first instance decision within the 12 month business target. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification. In 2025 the average processing time for all types of Join Family visa applications was 113 days. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I want to assure anyone who has made an application for a visa that my Department is doing everything possible to progress these applications as quickly as possible. In this context, the ongoing Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) modernisation programme is designed to support a more efficient, transparent and accessible immigration system. The recent establishment of dedicated teams for Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing are intended to help streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving the service delivery for join family visa applications. question: 1402. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding the number of join family visa application refusals that were successfully appealed in each of the years 2023, 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43072/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1396, 1397, 1398, 1399, 1400, 1401, 1402 and 1403 together. I can advise the Deputy that on 26 November 2025, Minister O'Callaghan and I published the review of the non-EEA Family Reunification Policy, which has remained largely unchanged since 2013, and sets out how Irish citizens and most non-EEA Irish residents may apply to bring non-EEA family members to live with them in Ireland. The revised Policy includes a number of changes, the majority of which took effect for new applications from 26 November, with longer term measures to be introduced as soon as operational considerations allow. The revised policy can be accessed on my Department’s website at the following link: (www.assets.gov.ie/static/documents/f88cb36e/Revised_Family_Reunification_Policy.pdf). Applications made before 26 November 2025 are assessed under the previous policy, which is available at the following link: (www.irishimmigration.ie/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Policy-document-on-Non-EEA-family-reunification.pdf) . I can advise the Deputy that my Department currently operates seven overseas Visa Offices in addition to the Visa Office in Dublin. These are located in Abuja, Beijing, London, Moscow, Ankara, Abu Dhabi and New Delhi. In addition, staff of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade process certain visa applications in Irish Embassies abroad under delegated authority from my Department. The current processing times of applications for join family visas varies depending on the circumstances when the application is made. If a non-EEA national is moving to Ireland because they have been granted a Critical Skills Employment Permit they can apply for join family visas at the same time as their own employment visa. When these visas are applied for together, they are processed in tandem and are typically completed in under eight weeks. My Department aims to process join family visa applications made in other circumstances within 12 months. I can assure the Deputy the majority of join family visas receive a first instance decision within the 12 month business target. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification. In 2025 the average processing time for all types of Join Family visa applications was 113 days. I understand that extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants, and I want to assure anyone who has made an application for a visa that my Department is doing everything possible to progress these applications as quickly as possible. The recent establishment of dedicated teams for Application Submission and Join Family Case Processing are intended to help streamline workflows, reduce duplication and strengthen expertise, thereby improving the service delivery for join family visa applications. question: 1405. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the measures he is taking to address migration (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43145/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1388 and 1405 together. Legal migration plays an essential and positive role in Ireland's society, as immigrants bring essential skills and experience that are much needed in the current labour market and are vital to addressing labour shortages. I am fully committed to ensuring that Ireland’s International Protection and immigration systems are robust, rules based and that the integrity of all our processes is maintained at all times. As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act was passed into law last month and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. My Department continues to focus on preparing for these new rules to take effect on 12 June 2026. The Pact will provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures and two months for processing applicants who have applied for protection elsewhere in Europe. Faster processing will mean that applicants spend less time in International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS) accommodation, and this will significantly reduce the cost of the asylum system to the State. Faster decision-making will also mean that successful applicants will be granted international protection sooner, and those whose applications are refused can be returned to their country of origin sooner. The enforcement aspects of our laws, including deportation orders, are an essential requirement for the system to work effectively and to ensure that there is confidence in the application of our legislation in this area. If a person does not remove themselves from the State following the issuance of a deportation order, they will be removed, and my Department has taken action to significantly improve immigration enforcement measures and increase removals. The number of deportation orders signed has increased in recent years. In 2024 (2,403) the number of orders signed increased by 180% compared to 2023 (857). In 2025, 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared to 2024. 2,108 deportation orders have been signed up to 05 June 2026. In 2024, 1,122 people departed from the State under various mechanisms (i.e. enforced deportation, voluntary return etc.). In 2025, 2,111 people had their departure confirmed through these pathways, an increase of 88% compared to 2024. Up to 05 June 2026, 977 people have departed the State through these pathways. The Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy detailing how Government intends to meet the demands, opportunities, and challenges facing Ireland’s society and economy over the next decade. My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of other Government departments to develop this strategy with the aim to publish Ireland’s first overarching whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy later this year. The scope of the Strategy will include issues such as labour market needs, legal pathways, international education and planning for public service provision including housing, amongst other issues relating to migration. To that end, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024 to support that work which now consists of ten Government Departments meeting at senior official level. The key objective of the Strategy and the SMPG is to develop a whole-of-government approach to migration policy that is coherent across Departments and responsive in seeking to address Ireland’s current and future demographic, economic and social policy needs. More broadly, capacity-based planning for Government services is a matter for each Department in its area of responsibility, be that Health, Education, Housing or any other sector, whether the demand for those services increases or declines in line with demographic changes, and whether those demographic changes arise from natural increases or declines in population or from immigration or emigration. The Government considers such matters at a central level in initiatives such as the National Development Plan and National Planning Framework, and via consideration at appropriate Cabinet Committees of capacity planning measures.

question: 1406. Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the Garda vetting card; the timeframe for this to go live; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43146/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The primary purpose of vetting carried out by the Garda National Vetting Bureau is to ensure the safety of children and vulnerable adults. Clearly, this requires a robust Garda vetting process that reassures the public, and in particular parents, that appropriate checks are conducted on people taking on positions of trust. The Government is aware of ongoing concerns regarding certain aspects of the vetting process and I have listened carefully to the views of affected sectors. I believe that the vetting system should be updated to ensure that the burden of seeking vetting disclosures, particularly on volunteers and organisations working in their communities, is minimised to the greatest extent possible, while maintaining the high standards that are necessary. Further to the work carried out by the Garda Vetting Review Group, steps are now being taken to implement a number of key changes to the process that will ensure it remains robust and effective while improving the service to customers. In practice, and subject to a general requirement that vetting be renewed every three years, it is envisaged that this will mean that when a person is vetted for the work they will be or are likely to be involved in as part of their employment or volunteering within identified risk categories, the person would not be required to repeat the process if they were to move to another role within the same risk category. My Department is actively engaging with the Garda National Vetting Bureau on the detailed work of developing the necessary legislative and technical steps to meet these goals in a way that is workable in practice. This includes an assessment of appropriate models for an expansion of digital service delivery, which is a very significant project that will necessarily take time to fully scope and implement.

question: 1408. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the full breakdown of the €148,253,530 purchase price including VAT for a facility (details supplied); the valuation methodology used; the independent valuations obtained prior to Cabinet approval in June 2025; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43199/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 1408, 1409, 1410, 1411, 1412, 1413, 1414, 1415, 1416 and 1417 together. Government policy is to develop more State-owned international protection accommodation, to assist in reducing the current degree of reliance on commercial provision in this sector. The purchase of the Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre in 2025 was an important step in this strategy, and increased State-owned beds to 4,000 in 2025, compared to 900 in early 2024. Capacity on the site is approximately 2,300, with a mix of international protection and Ukraine accommodation provided. The Citywest facility is a key component in the State's implementation of the EU Migration Pact this year, acting as a screening centre and border procedure location as required under the Pact. The full purchase price (including VAT) for the Citywest property was €148,253,530 and represents significant value for the State. The purchase will significantly reduce the current expenditure on State accommodation at this site over the coming years and increase the value for public money now and for the future. The payback period on the purchase price is approximately 4 years, due to the reduced running costs of a State-owned facility compared to the previous leasing model. The purchase was funded from Vote 24 Justice, Home Affairs and Migration under the Subhead Programme C5 International Protection Seekers Accommodation. The capital allocation was increased from €40 million to €153.3 million in the Further Revised Estimate presented by the Minister to Dáil Éireann in September 2025, to allow for the full cost of the purchase of Citywest. This was completed in compliance with Public Financial Procedures including Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation sanction procedures and Government Infrastructure Guidelines, which set out clear guidelines for the evaluation, planning, and management of public investment projects, including purchase or acquisitions of State assets of this kind. Citywest is recorded as an asset in the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration fixed asset register and will be reported in the Appropriation Accounts 2025 for the Vote 24 Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. Citywest has been successfully used as a processing centre and accommodation centre since 2022, with registration services provided to both people applying for Temporary Protection due to war in Ukraine, and to people applying for international protection. The former Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre have been in State ownership since August 2025. The department has contracted a service provider on it's behalf to provide services on site. The State has been responsible for management and oversight of the International Protection and Temporary Protection services provided on the campus at all times since services commenced in 2022. A 12-month transitional service agreement was put in place with the existing provider to ensure operational continuity. The transitional service agreement includes an optional six month extension and it is anticipated that it will be necessary to utilise the six month extension to allow adequate time to complete a compliant procurement process. While the department treats details of contracts and rate as commercially sensitive, the nightly contracted cost for accommodation post-purchase represents improved value for money for the State. The purchase of the site and overall expenditure on accommodation will form part of the 2025 Appropriation Account in due course, which will be subject to audit by the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG). A community engagement process was initiated following the Government’s approval to purchase the former Citywest Hotel and Convention Centre for the provision of accommodation for people seeking international protection. The engagement process ensures that the department knows the issues that have been identified at local level, by community representatives, to best support planning for essential supports and services. The new International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and was passed into law last month. The new rules will take effect later this week from 12 June 2026. Reforming and speeding up processing of applications should also serve over time to reduce the scale of the demand for international protection accommodation.
