This programme commenced in 2020 with the approval of a multi-year business plan and is currently in the third of its four implementation phases. The fourth phase is scheduled to commence this year. Efficiency related projects under this programme include the roll out of video link and technologically enabled courtrooms, the phased rollout of a Unified Case Management System (UCMS), various data sharing projects within the Criminal Justice Sector to improve efficiencies between state bodies and a new online jury system to remove significant paper handling activities in processing the jury summons process. The Courts Service has continued the expansion of video link and technologically enabled courtrooms, providing remote courts and digital evidence display functionality. Video technology is now available in 175 courtrooms, increased from 46 at the start of 2020.

question: 1457. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is aware that according to a report (details supplied), the number of prisoners held on remand in Ireland increased by 34% between 2019 and 2024; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [44040/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, it is not open to me to comment or intervene in relation to how particular court proceedings are conducted, or on the outcome of those proceedings. These are matters entirely for the presiding judge. The Irish Prison Service must accept into custody all people committed to prison by the courts. However, I am also committed to implementing policies aimed at increasing the use of community sanctions, reducing offending, diverting people away from the criminal justice system, and providing more effective rehabilitation. These policies aim to contribute to the effective management of prison numbers and increasing the availability of cost-effective criminal justice responses for minor offences. In relation to bail, I am committed to ensuring our bail laws are fit for purpose. It must be remembered that while our bail laws provide for the refusal of bail in particular circumstances, the presiding judge is entirely independent in the exercise of their judicial functions, and the decision to grant bail in a particular case is solely a matter for the judge. The report completed by Mr Lorcan Staines SC ‘An Assessment of the Efficacy of Bail Laws in Ireland’ was published by my Department in November 2025. This examination of our bail laws and subsequent proposals underlines the need for additional actions to be considered, to ensure the criminal justice system effectively mitigates against risks that may be associated with individuals on bail. A number of the recommendations are under active consideration, or already in the process of being implemented, across my Department. The Programme for Government commits to implement electronic tagging for appropriate categories of people including those who would otherwise be remanded in custody. Under Budget 2026 funding of €2.1 million was allocated for the project to allow for staffing, procurement, and other set-up costs. A pilot is expected to be operational in 2026.

question: 1458. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of deaths of persons in the custody of Cork prison in each of the years 2021 to 2025 and to date in 2026, including deaths occurring in the prison, in hospital, and deaths occurring within one month of a grant of temporary release, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [44041/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I would firstly like to express my sympathies to the family and friends of each of those individuals who have died in prison custody. All deaths of prisoners within prisons are notified to An Garda Síochána, who investigate where circumstances warrant, in addition to the inquest held in the Coroner's Court. The cause of death is determined by a jury on the basis of the information presented to the Coroner's Court. All prisoner deaths, including deaths that occur within one month of temporary release are subject to an independent investigation by the Office of the Inspector of Prisons. Finalised reports and any associated Prison Service Action Plan to address recommendations contained in the report are published in an anonymised form on the Gov.ie website and made available to the Coroner. In addition, the Irish Prison Service has a robust, internal review mechanism which assesses the circumstances of each prisoner death, highlights accountability and actions taken in relation to it, and outlines any lessons learned. Table 1 attached, outlines the number of deaths of those in custody in Cork Prison between 2021 to 2025. Please note there are no deaths recorded in Cork Prison to date in 2026. The data includes deaths occurring in prison, in hospital, and deaths occurring within one month of temporary release. question: 1459. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of recorded prisoner-on-prisoner assaults; the number of recorded assaults on staff in Cork Prison in each of the years 2021 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [44042/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am advised by the Irish Prison Service that the number of direct physical assaults involving prisoner-on-prisoner and prisoner-on-staff between 2021 and 2025 is detailed in the attached table. Please note the figures for staff includes but is not limited to prison officers. *Figures for direct physical assaults involving prisoner-on-prisoner and prisoner-on-staff are not currently available for 2026 as these require validation following the year end. The 2026 figures will be published on the Irish Prison Service’s website in 2027. Every assault on a member of staff is treated as serious and appropriate action is taken. Staff who are subject to an assault or threat in a prison are given the necessary supports through the Employee Assistance Programme. Section 19 of the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994 as amended specifically provides for assaults or threats to peace officers, including prison officers acting in the execution of their duty. Any person who assaults or threatens to assault a peace officer in the execution of their duty is guilty of an offence. The maximum penalty available for assaulting a peace officer, including prison officers, was increased from 7 years to 12 years in the Criminal Justice (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2023, which came into effect in November 2023. This sends a very clear message that attacks on frontline workers will not be tolerated and will be dealt with robustly. The Irish Prison Service established a Violence Management Steering Group in 2025 as a result of observations communicated by the European Committee for the Reduction of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (“CPT”) during its eighth periodic visit to Ireland. The group aims to reduce violence in all its forms across the Irish Prison Service, and ensure that effective response mechanisms are in place. These measures are designed to improve the safety of all staff, prisoners, visitors and contractors from threats, aggression, physical assaults and other types of violent behaviours. question: 1460. Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of meetings of the Standing Committee on the Provision of Coroner-Directed Post Mortem Examination Services held since its establishment in April 2022; the recommendations made by the committee; and the actions taken by his Department arising from those recommendations. [44104/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The post-mortem examination service, which supports the work of the Coroner Service, is supported by several departments and agencies. My Department is responsible for the legislation underpinning the work of coroners, while the provision of the post-mortem examination service is largely provided through the health service and its personnel. Where a post-mortem examination is deemed to be required, the coroner will arrange for it to be conducted as expeditiously as possible in order to ensure the timely release of remains to the next of kin of the deceased. Securing the provision of the post-mortem examination service for the coronial death investigation function is challenging and I have been engaging with the Minister for Health to address this. There are issues arising within the pathology profession, including relating to training and recruitment, as well as competing demands on pathologists in areas of diagnostic and research work. I acknowledge those concerns. In 2022, my Department established a ‘Standing Committee on the Provision of Coroner Directed Post-mortem Examination Services', membership of which is drawn from my Department, other relevant Government Departments, including the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive, the Office of the State Pathologist, the Coroners Society of Ireland, and the Faculty of Pathology at the Royal College of Physicians Ireland. The role of the Standing Committee is to identify and consider the core issues involved in the provision of a sustainable and professional histopathology post-mortem service for coroner-directed PMEs. The committee has provided valuable insight into the complex issues involved in the provision of coroner-directed post-mortem services. The committee is chaired by my Department but the work of the committee is inherently cross-departmental in nature and therefore committee members report to multiple parent Departments. The valuable work of the committee has informed my engagement with Minister for Health in seeking to resolve the complex issues that arise within the health sector, in order to secure a sustainable solution. The committee has met thirteen times and the next meeting is scheduled for the end of this month. While this committee is an important forum with appropriate membership to discuss issues in relation to the autopsy service, the situation in University Hospital Waterford (UHW) reached a critical juncture in January this year when pathologists employed at that location indicated that they were no longer available to carry out post-mortem examinations. Coroner directed post-mortem examinations for counties Waterford, Wexford, Kilkenny, Carlow, and Tipperary are carried out in UHW. My Department has introduced a short-term solution where locum pathologists are providing a coronial post-mortem examination service on a three-day per week rota since 1 January in UHW. This approach is necessary to minimise any impact on bereaved family members who would otherwise experience lengthy wait times for the release of remains which are the subject of coroners’ inquiries. However, the use of locum pathologists to conduct coroner directed post-mortem examinations is not a long-term solution to these issues and my Department is aware that a more sustainable solution is required in this regard.

question: 1461. Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department will consider potential criminal involvement in occupation, apartheid and genocide in the service of the IDF as a disqualifying factor to receive a visa to enter Ireland. [44174/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I can advise the Deputy that Israeli citizens are not visa required for Ireland and therefore do not need to apply to the Immigration Service of my Department for a visa prior to travel. As with all non-EEA nationals seeking entry to the State, an Immigration Officer must determine whether that person should be granted leave to land in accordance with the Immigration Act 2004. In performing their duties, an Officer is required to consider all of the relevant circumstances of the individual at the time. Section 4(3) of the Immigration Act 2004 sets out the grounds on which a person may be refused permission to enter the State. These include, but are not limited to, previous criminal convictions and where a person's entry into, or presence in, the State could pose a threat to national security or be contrary to public policy.

question: 1756. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Health the actions her Department is taking to address the acute national shortage of dental nurses within the oral healthcare sector; if she has engaged with the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment to support the removal of dental nurses from the ineligible list of occupations to allow for general employment permits; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [41475/26]
answer: Minister for Health It is heartening to note that as of the 26th of May 2026, there are now 953 active registrants on the Register of Dental Nurses. This has increased since June last year, there are now an additional 41 registered dental nurses. The Council of European Chief Dental Officers data on oral healthcare workforce from 2021 indicates there were an estimated 4,900 dental nurses in the Ireland noting that registration is voluntary for dental nurses. My Department supports any expansion in the oral healthcare workforce and has worked with the Education and Training Boards to convert the Dental Nurse Traineeship into a National Apprenticeship Programme to support the training of the next generation of dental nurses for our oral healthcare workforce. I am pleased to inform the Deputy that on the 4th of March this year the Further Education and Training College in Cathal Brugha City of Dublin Education and Training Board has been validated for the Higher Certificate in Dental Nursing Apprenticeship which is due to commence this September. This will enhance the number of dental nurses and is in line with expanding our oral health workforce. The approval of this apprenticeship scheme complements the work that my Department is progressing with colleagues in the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (DFHERIS) regarding the expansion of training places for oral healthcare professionals including dental nurses. In that context, I understand that officials from DFHERIS are engaging with University College Cork to discuss in detail its proposal to establish a community-based dental outreach centre in North Cork, and to advance this important project. The proposal, which includes a request for capital investment from my Department will support an increase in undergraduate capacity in dentistry, dental hygiene and dental nursing training places. My Department has also received a draft proposal to increase training places for oral healthcare professionals including dental nurses at the Dublin Dental University Hospital at Trinity College Dublin. This will require further discussion to progress this proposal with the aim to maximise the benefit this proposal will have in terms of increasing the number of oral healthcare professionals in Ireland, as well as increased service provision. Alongside this, engagement with DFHERIS and the Higher Education Authority is ongoing to expand our oral healthcare workforce capacity in a sustainable and strategic manner, as well as exploring capacity regionally across the Technological University sector. My Department does acknowledge the important and effective role the employment permit system plays in meeting the skills and labour shortages in the State from a health perspective, on a short-term basis. However, it is not clear how employment permit holders can address the shortage of dental nurses within the oral healthcare sector. Reform of work permit regulations to allow non-European Economic Area (EEA) nationals to work in Ireland - including dental nurses - falls within the remit of the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. Workers coming to Ireland from outside the EU are required to obtain employment permits. The Department of Enterprise Trade and Employment (DETE) operates the employment permits system in accordance with the Employment Permits Act 2024. The employment permits legislation sets out various criteria that must be met when considering a permit application, including immigration permission, testing of the labour market, minimum annual remuneration and minimum ratio of EEA employees to non-EEA employees. The Ineligible Occupations List consists of occupations for which there is an adequate supply of labour and skills, and for which an employment permit will not be issued. Currently dental nurses are on the Ineligible Occupations List. Any proposal advocating removing dental nurses from the Ineligible Occupations List will be considered subject to the receipt of an evidence-based and data-driven submission.

question: 2343. Deputy Pádraig Rice asked the Minister for Health if the review of access to cannabis for medical use is examining barriers to clinician participation in the Medical Cannabis Access Programme, including prescribing pathways, education, and administrative processes; if her Department envisages a future role for general practitioners in supporting continuity of care for patients prescribed medicinal cannabis products, including the management of repeat prescribing in appropriate cases; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [43683/26]
answer: Minister for Health Under Statutory Instrument No. 262/2019 - Misuse Of Drugs (Prescription And Control Of Supply Of Cannabis For Medical Use) Regulations 2019, the legislative basis for the MCAP a specified controlled drug is defined as a cannabis product or preparation— (a) which is produced from dried, ground or powdered flower of Cannabis, (b) which is not a medicinal product which is the subject of a marketing authorisation within the meaning assigned to that term in Regulation 3(1) of the Medicinal Products (Control of Placing on the Market) Regulations 2007 ( S.I. No. 540 of 2007 ). This means these products are not authorised medicines with a marketing authorisation that have gone through the normal testing and safety processes required of a medicine. Accordingly in Part 2 of the Regulations restrictions on issuing of prescriptions for specified controlled drugs are set out, including 4. (1) A practitioner shall not issue a prescription for a specified controlled drug other than where— (a) the practitioner is a medical consultant, (b) the practitioner’s name and address are included on the prescription, and (c) treatment with the specified controlled drug remains under the supervision of that practitioner. There are no current plans to alter the practice of consultant-only prescribing.

question: 2501. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether their Department, the Higher Education Authority, or any body under their aegis has undertaken an assessment of the number of Irish-qualified graduates working abroad in healthcare and other critical skills sectors; whether estimates are available by profession, qualification type and destination country; whether any analysis has been conducted of graduate emigration, return migration, retention rates or workforce losses within five years of qualification; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [43656/26]
answer: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science The outcomes of graduates from Irish Higher Education Institutions (HEIs), including outcomes relating to international mobility, can be tracked through two published sources: the Higher Education Authority’s (HEA) Graduate Outcomes Survey (GOS) and the Central Statistics Offices (CSO) Educational Longitudinal Database (ELD). The GOS is an annual survey which looks at the main activity of graduates from Irish HEIs (i.e. Employment, Further Study, Seeking Employment, or Other) nine months after graduation. The latest survey relates to the graduating class of 2024. The survey results relating to graduates in employment can be broken down by location of employment (i.e., in Ireland or overseas), field of study, and degree level. For the 2024 graduate cohort, 90.8% were employed in Ireland nine months after graduating while 9.2% were employed overseas. For graduates from Health and Welfare related degrees the proportion employed overseas was 5.8%. It should be noted that the proportion of graduates working overseas varies significantly depending on the graduates’ primary domicile and that these figures represent a point in time, as migration can often be temporary. The proportion of Irish domiciled Health and Welfare graduates (from the 2024 graduate cohort) working overseas nine months after graduating was 2.3%. The table below shows the proportion of the 2024 graduate cohort employed overseas nine months after graduating, by field of study and degree level, across all domiciles. Graduates from Irish HEIs in 2024 Field of study Undergraduate Postgraduate All graduates Social Sciences, journalism and information 7.9% 19.9% 13.8% Agriculture, forestry, fisheries and veterinary 15.3% 10.2% 12.6% Arts and humanities 8.4% 23.0% 12.1% Business, administration and law 9.0% 14.3% 11.3% Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs) 8.0% 13.2% 10.5% Engineering, manufacturing and construction 8.0% 11.0% 9.2% Natural sciences, mathematics and statistics 6.3% 14.1% 8.7% Services 8.2% 7.0% 7.5% Health and welfare 4.4% 8.5% 5.8% Education 1.3% 4.5% 3.0% All fields of study 7.1% 12.6% 9.2% Table Source: HEA Graduate Outcomes Survey The CSOs ELD also provides data on graduates from Irish HEIs. This is a statistical framework that matches data from sources such as the HEA, Revenue, and the Department of Social Protection to examine learner outcomes and provide a mechanism to track long-term migration patterns, including return dynamics. A recent publication based on this data was the CSOs “Higher Education Outcomes – Health Graduates 2023” report which examines the outcomes of graduates from Health related programmes at Irish HEIs for up to 10 years post graduation, broken out by degree field. This data includes both Irish and Internationally domiciled graduates. Key findings from this report include: • 37% of all nursing and midwifery graduates from the 2013 graduate cohort are estimated to have emigrated at some point during the period 2013 to 2022, with 62% of these returning within the same period. • 30% of all medicine graduates from the 2013 graduate cohort are estimated to have emigrated for at least one year in the 10 years since they graduated, with 39% of these returning within the same period.
